# Todo

This file contains near term tasks with a short description
and reference links to more details.

Intro paragraphs in `## Todo` and `## Bugs` should begin every
line with 1 leading space so they don't match the `^\d+\. `
pattern that locates numbered entries; 2 or 3 spaces also work.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text **moves** here
(never copied; one home per text). The picked-up task is a
`###` heading; a multi-cycle program adds one level, where the
program is the `###` and its current stage a `####` (headings
give the current work durable anchors, which numbered Todo
entries can't). The problem overview is followed by the
"plan", a bulleted list of the development "ladder". Each
rung is prepended with its commit reference, a literal
`[[N]]` placeholder until the commit is pushed, then
backfilled to a real file-local `[[n]]` ref (same pattern as
the chores As-built rungs):
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y close-out and validation

### Refactor: typed jj facade -> jj-lib in-process; end subprocess spawning

Version-control operations were ~30 hand-rolled `run("jj", ...)`
spawns plus every mutation, with per-module private wrappers
and raw-git vestiges in init: stderr parsing instead of typed
errors, and jj's single-attempt index-lock acquisition (the
push `bookmark-set` lock race in [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md))
can't be retried where it fails. A multi-ladder program; the
staged plan, design detail, and the eight absorbed former
Todos live in
[refactor-20260716.md](notes/refactor-20260716.md).

Program ladder in **straight trunk order**, one bullet per
commit that lands on the branch, so reading it top to bottom
is reading `git log --first-parent`. `refactor:` entries are
the program's rungs, one per cycle (adjacent stages
consolidated 2026-07-24; titles are the anticipated close-out
titles; unshipped versions are provisional, since jj-lib may
split into two cycles). `docs:` entries are interludes that
sit between cycles and belong to no rung. Every shipped ref
points at a close-out commit on `refactor-vc-x1`, treated as
permanent: the branch is long-lived and lands on main
merge-only, never rebased.

The order is load-bearing: a
trapezoid's `<base>` is the parent of its own first rung, not
the previous close-out, so 0.78.0 bases on 0.77.2. Taking the
close-out instead swallows the interludes into the merge's
ladder side, which already bit at 0.76.0, whose base was the
0.75.1 interlude. See
[the recipe](notes/cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe).

     settle the version-coupling policy and record it; `-2`
     reads via jj-lib; `-3` mutations + the deferred `@`
     reads; `-4` index-lock retry (bugs.md #1) with a

388	
389	Commits: [[8]]
390	
391	A trunk-line interlude between `0.77.0` and the punctuation
392	cycle, carrying two threads from the 2026-07-29 session plus
393	the corrections the `0.77.0` close-out earned by attempting
394	the trapezoid recipe as written.
395	
396	- The op-store coexistence risk was a stub asking for a spike;
397	  it is now answered, and the answer is "unenforceable,
398	  probably fine". Read out of jj-lib 0.41 source against an
399	  installed jj 0.40.0: structural change fails closed, the
400	  index self-heals by reindexing, the op store serializes with
401	  protobuf and carries no version stamp, and jj publishes no
402	  on-disk compatibility policy. We think the residual risk is
403	  low-probability, silent, and low-blast-radius.
404	- The mitigation that looked obvious does not work. A
405	  `jj --version` gate samples what `$PATH` resolves to, which
406	  says nothing about the jj an editor integration or a later
407	  session runs against the same repo. This workspace already
408	  has two.
409	- Consequence for the ladder: taking the coupling is a
410	  decision, not a step 0.78.0 can assume. The index-lock prize
411	  (bugs.md #1) does not require it, since a retry can wrap the
412	  existing spawn today.
413	- The trapezoid recipe's step 4 is `jj git push`, not
414	  `vc-x1 push`. Push runs its whole pipeline or none of it,
415	  and the bot repo is never quiet: by the time the reshape is
416	  done, `.claude` holds the session writes from steps 1-3, so
417	  `commit-bot` wants a title for a work-side publish that
418	  needs nothing but a moved ref.
419	
420	## docs: typeable punctuation
421	
422	Commits:
423	
424	`—`, `–`, `…` and `→` cost nothing to write and are paid on
425	every read: none can be typed at a terminal, so none can be
426	grepped for, and an em dash next to option syntax reads as
427	another flag. Nobody chose the 551 sites across the five prose
428	files, they accumulated. AGENTS.md gains the rule that bans
429	them, and the sweep converts what is already written.
430	
431	One commit, no ladder: the rule and the sweep are one idea,
432	and per-file rungs would buy no review value in prose files
433	that have no build and no tests.
434	
435	It started as a question about whether a ladder rung's title
436	and its detail should share a line. They should not, and the
437	em dash was what let them: it joins two things without naming
438	their relationship, which is the failure `### Semicolons
439	inside bullets` already names for `;`. Pulling that thread
440	reached the character itself, and then the whole class. The
441	rule is `### Typeable punctuation only` under
442	[Prose form](/AGENTS.md#prose-form), a sibling to the semicolon
443	rule and cross-linked from its intro. It was designed jointly
444	with the iiac-perf project, whose AGENTS.md carries the same
445	section.
446	
447	### Three roles a banned character can play
448	
449	The rule took four rounds to get right, and each round was the
450	same mistake in a different place: a blanket claim that the
451	next paragraph then contradicted. The settled form sorts by
452	what the character is *doing*, not where it sits.
453	
454	- **Naming it** (`` `…` ``) is a specimen and stays. This is
455	  how the section names the characters it bans.
456	- **Doing a job** (`` `.expect(…)` ``) is a use and converts.
457	  A first draft exempted all code spans, which would have
458	  forbidden the very conversions the sweep had just made.
459	- **Transcribed from outside** (tool output, an error message,
460	  an already-published commit title) keeps its characters,
461	  code span or not. Transcription is not authoring.
462	
463	The third role is why `README.md` still holds four em dashes:
464	its `vc-x1 config` samples transcribe what the installed binary
465	prints, and `src/config_schema.rs` puts em dashes in the `doc:`
466	strings. Converting the samples would make the docs claim
467	output that does not exist. They convert at `0.77.3`, in the
468	same commit that changes the strings.
469	
470	We think the reason this rule needs to be absolute where the
471	semicolon rule is a lean is that the cost is asymmetric: an em
472	dash is free to write and paid on every read, so a soft rule
473	accumulates them. 551 sites in five files is the evidence.
474	
475	### Four banned characters, and an audit that checked three
476	
477	The rule bans four characters: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`. Every
478	verification run during the sweep counted three of them. The en
479	dash was never in the audit command, so it was never in the
480	report, so the sweep read as complete while two real sites
481	survived: a section range written `1–8` in TODO.md and a step
482	range written `1–3` in cycle-protocol.md. Both were found by
483	the last check
484	before the commit, which happened to include the fourth
485	character.
486	
487	We think the en dash is the easiest of the four to miss for a
488	reason that will recur: it is the only one with no distinct
489	visual signature at a glance. `…` and `→` are unmistakable, and
490	an em dash is long enough to notice in running prose, but `–`
491	between two numbers looks exactly like the hyphen it should
492	have been. It hides in precisely the construct it is used for.
493	
494	Two consequences worth carrying forward:
495	
496	- **The audit must enumerate the ban, not a memory of it.** A
497	  check that tracks a subset silently reports success. This is
498	  the same defect class as the `clippy ... | tail -2 && cargo
499	  test` gate found at the 0.77.0 close-out, where the pipeline
500	  status came from `tail` and the `&&` was decorative: a
501	  mechanism that looks like a guarantee and is not.
502	- **A future `validate-repo` byte scan should read its
503	  character set from one place** shared with the rule's text,
504	  so the two cannot drift. Enumerating the characters a second
505	  time in the checker recreates exactly the gap this cycle hit.
506	
507	The count reported for this cycle, 551 sites, is therefore two
508	low as originally tallied; the corrected total is 553.
509	
510	### An em dash in a heading moves its anchor
511	
512	Found mid-sweep, and it is the one silent failure in the whole
513	change. Stripping the dash leaves the spaces on both sides, so
514	`## A — B` slugs to `#a--b` while the colon form slugs to
515	`#a-b`. Converting a heading therefore breaks every inbound
516	link to it.
517	
518	Three headings in AGENTS.md and one in refactor-20260716.md
519	were affected; a repo-wide grep found four inbound links, all
520	in the same files. The rule now carries the warning.

## docs: typeable punctuation

Commits:

`—`, `–`, `…` and `→` cost nothing to write and are paid on
every read: none can be typed at a terminal, so none can be
grepped for, and an em dash next to option syntax reads as
another flag. Nobody chose the 551 sites across the five prose
files, they accumulated. AGENTS.md gains the rule that bans
them, and the sweep converts what is already written.

One commit, no ladder: the rule and the sweep are one idea,
and per-file rungs would buy no review value in prose files
that have no build and no tests.

It started as a question about whether a ladder rung's title
and its detail should share a line. They should not, and the
em dash was what let them: it joins two things without naming
their relationship, which is the failure `### Semicolons
inside bullets` already names for `;`. Pulling that thread
reached the character itself, and then the whole class. The
rule is `### Typeable punctuation only` under
[Prose form](/AGENTS.md#prose-form), a sibling to the semicolon
rule and cross-linked from its intro. It was designed jointly
with the iiac-perf project, whose AGENTS.md carries the same
section.

### Three roles a banned character can play

The rule took four rounds to get right, and each round was the
same mistake in a different place: a blanket claim that the
next paragraph then contradicted. The settled form sorts by
what the character is *doing*, not where it sits.

- **Naming it** (`` `…` ``) is a specimen and stays. This is
  how the section names the characters it bans.
- **Doing a job** (`` `.expect(…)` ``) is a use and converts.
  A first draft exempted all code spans, which would have
  forbidden the very conversions the sweep had just made.
- **Transcribed from outside** (tool output, an error message,
  an already-published commit title) keeps its characters,
  code span or not. Transcription is not authoring.

The third role is why `README.md` still holds four em dashes:
its `vc-x1 config` samples transcribe what the installed binary
prints, and `src/config_schema.rs` puts em dashes in the `doc:`
strings. Converting the samples would make the docs claim
output that does not exist. They convert at `0.77.3`, in the
same commit that changes the strings.

We think the reason this rule needs to be absolute where the
semicolon rule is a lean is that the cost is asymmetric: an em
dash is free to write and paid on every read, so a soft rule
accumulates them. 551 sites in five files is the evidence.

### Four banned characters, and an audit that checked three

The rule bans four characters: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`. Every
verification run during the sweep counted three of them. The en
dash was never in the audit command, so it was never in the
report, so the sweep read as complete while two real sites
survived: a section range written `1–8` in TODO.md and a step
range written `1–3` in cycle-protocol.md. Both were found by
the last check
before the commit, which happened to include the fourth
character.

We think the en dash is the easiest of the four to miss for a
reason that will recur: it is the only one with no distinct
visual signature at a glance. `…` and `→` are unmistakable, and
an em dash is long enough to notice in running prose, but `–`
between two numbers looks exactly like the hyphen it should
have been. It hides in precisely the construct it is used for.

Two consequences worth carrying forward:

- **The audit must enumerate the ban, not a memory of it.** A
  check that tracks a subset silently reports success. This is
  the same defect class as the `clippy ... | tail -2 && cargo
  test` gate found at the 0.77.0 close-out, where the pipeline
  status came from `tail` and the `&&` was decorative: a
  mechanism that looks like a guarantee and is not.
- **A future `validate-repo` byte scan should read its
  character set from one place** shared with the rule's text,
  so the two cannot drift. Enumerating the characters a second
  time in the checker recreates exactly the gap this cycle hit.

The count reported for this cycle, 551 sites, is therefore two
low as originally tallied; the corrected total is 553.

### An em dash in a heading moves its anchor

Found mid-sweep, and it is the one silent failure in the whole
change. Stripping the dash leaves the spaces on both sides, so
`## A — B` slugs to `#a--b` while the colon form slugs to
`#a-b`. Converting a heading therefore breaks every inbound
link to it.

Three headings in AGENTS.md and one in refactor-20260716.md
were affected; a repo-wide grep found four inbound links, all
in the same files. The rule now carries the warning.

441	**Step 4 is not a `vc-x1 push`** (corrected at the `0.77.0`
442	close-out, which tried it). Push runs its whole pipeline or
443	none of it, and the bot repo is never quiet for long: by the
444	time the reshape is done, `.claude` holds the session writes
445	from steps 1-3, so `commit-bot` wants to run and the message
446	stage demands a title for it. The result is a bot-side
447	requirement blocking a work-side publish that needs nothing
448	but a moved ref. Publishing an already-made commit is a
449	different operation from committing and publishing, and only
450	the latter is push's job.
451	
452	#### Details
453	
454	- **Verify two parents before step 4.** `jj log -r <closeout>
455	  -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
456	  both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>`
457	  is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at `0.74.0`, `0.75.0`,
458	  `0.76.0`), but a collapsed merge is indistinguishable from
459	  a correct one in `jj log --no-graph` and is only visible
460	  once published.
461	- **`<base>` is not always the previous close-out.** A docs
462	  or planning interlude between cycles sits on the trunk line
463	  and must stay there; take the parent of the ladder's first
464	  rung, not the last close-out.
465	- **Step 3 is about `@`, not the bookmark.** The bookmark
466	  follows the rewrite in step 2 on its own. What step 2
467	  leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r`
468	  re-parents descendants onto the rebased commit's **old**
469	  parent, so the empty `@` from step 1 lands beside the merge
470	  on `<tip>`, and the working tree reverts to pre-close-out
471	  content, which looks alarming and isn't. `jj new` puts `@`
472	  back on top of the merge so the tree is right and the next
473	  commit continues from there. Skipping it doesn't break the
474	  publish; it leaves you working from the wrong parent.
475	- **Trailers survive.** The reshape changes `<closeout>`'s
476	  SHA but not its change ID, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped
477	  in step 1 stay valid in both directions. This is why the
478	  reshape is safe after the trailers are written.
479	- **Step 4 moves the bookmark sideways.** Step 1's SHA
480	  becomes unreachable; anyone who fetched between the two
481	  pushes holds a dangling commit. Consequently a
482	  [`Commits:` backfill](#commits-backfill) must never read a
483	  SHA from that window; wait until step 4 lands.
484	- **Immutability.** No flag is needed on a long-lived topic
485	  bookmark. Only when `<closeout>` is already on `trunk()`
486	  does the rebase need `--ignore-immutable`, and then the
487	  push force-updates the target.
488	- **The bot repo is left for afterwards.** Step 4 touches only
489	  the work repo, so `.claude` still holds every session write
490	  from the whole procedure. `vc-x1 squash-push` folds that
491	  tail into the bot commit, and its change id survives the
492	  squash, so the work-side `ochid:` keeps resolving.
493

**Step 4 is not a `vc-x1 push`** (corrected at the `0.77.0`
close-out, which tried it). Push runs its whole pipeline or
none of it, and the bot repo is never quiet for long: by the
time the reshape is done, `.claude` holds the session writes
from steps 1-3, so `commit-bot` wants to run and the message
stage demands a title for it. The result is a bot-side
requirement blocking a work-side publish that needs nothing
but a moved ref. Publishing an already-made commit is a
different operation from committing and publishing, and only
the latter is push's job.

#### Details

- **Verify two parents before step 4.** `jj log -r <closeout>
  -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
  both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>`
  is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at `0.74.0`, `0.75.0`,
  `0.76.0`), but a collapsed merge is indistinguishable from
  a correct one in `jj log --no-graph` and is only visible
  once published.
- **`<base>` is not always the previous close-out.** A docs
  or planning interlude between cycles sits on the trunk line
  and must stay there; take the parent of the ladder's first
  rung, not the last close-out.
- **Step 3 is about `@`, not the bookmark.** The bookmark
  follows the rewrite in step 2 on its own. What step 2
  leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r`
  re-parents descendants onto the rebased commit's **old**
  parent, so the empty `@` from step 1 lands beside the merge
  on `<tip>`, and the working tree reverts to pre-close-out
  content, which looks alarming and isn't. `jj new` puts `@`
  back on top of the merge so the tree is right and the next
  commit continues from there. Skipping it doesn't break the
  publish; it leaves you working from the wrong parent.
- **Trailers survive.** The reshape changes `<closeout>`'s
  SHA but not its change ID, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped
  in step 1 stay valid in both directions. This is why the
  reshape is safe after the trailers are written.
- **Step 4 moves the bookmark sideways.** Step 1's SHA
  becomes unreachable; anyone who fetched between the two
  pushes holds a dangling commit. Consequently a
  [`Commits:` backfill](#commits-backfill) must never read a
  SHA from that window; wait until step 4 lands.
- **Immutability.** No flag is needed on a long-lived topic
  bookmark. Only when `<closeout>` is already on `trunk()`
  does the rebase need `--ignore-immutable`, and then the
  push force-updates the target.
- **The bot repo is left for afterwards.** Step 4 touches only
  the work repo, so `.claude` still holds every session write
  from the whole procedure. `vc-x1 squash-push` folds that
  tail into the bot commit, and its change id survives the
  squash, so the work-side `ochid:` keeps resolving.

#### Recovery

- **Nothing is published between steps 2 and 3**, so the local
  reshape is undoable with `jj undo` / `jj op restore`.
- **A collapsed or mis-parented merge** (step 2 verification
  fails): undo and redo step 2 with the corrected revisions.

Agreed on both splits. But before you commit to "everywhere in one change," here is what "everywhere" actually is — I counted the whole repo, not just `src/`:

| area | sites |
|---|---|
| `notes/chores/chores-01..15.md` | 1965 |
| `src/` (+ `tests/`) | ~875 |
| other `notes/*.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `support/` | ~805 |
| **total** | **3645** |

The 0.77.2 sweep converted five prose files. `notes/` at large, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, and the entire chores archive were never in scope — `versioning.md` alone still has 33, and I hit them while reading it just now.

## Two reasons the chores archive can't ride in a mechanical sweep

**Transcription.** The three-roles rule says text quoted from outside this repo's prose keeps its characters. In `src/` that case is rare. In `chores/` it is everywhere: pasted tool output, quoted error messages, already-published commit titles that must stay byte-identical for `git log --grep`. A sed over 1965 sites would silently corrupt the transcriptions, and it would do so in the one place where the corrupted text is a historical record nobody will re-derive. That is not a sweep, it is 1965 judgment calls.

**Anchors.** Converting a heading moves its slug, and the chores files are the most linked-into surface in the repo — every `[N]:` ref from `TODO.md`, `done.md`, and the refactor notes points at a `chores-NN.md#anchor`. A repo-wide heading conversion breaks inbound links at a scale where the "re-point in the same commit" instruction stops being checkable by eye.

There is also a policy wrinkle: the rule as written says *"It applies going forward; existing text converts when touched."* Sweeping the historical archive isn't executing that rule, it's amending it. Fine to amend — but it should be a stated decision in the same commit, not an implied one.

## What I'd actually do

Split by *risk*, not by directory, and the split falls in a natural place:

- **One change, all live surfaces**: `src/` + `tests/` + all non-chores `notes/*.md` + `ARCHITECTURE.md` + `support/`. ~1680 sites. These are edited and grepped, which is the rule's whole justification. Includes the user-visible strings, so the cargo cycle is mandatory and the four README `vc-x1 config` samples regenerate after `cargo install` in that same commit. Your instinct is right here — this is one idea, and per-file rungs would buy nothing, exactly as chores-15 argued for 0.77.2.
- **The chores archive stays under "converts when touched"**, or becomes its own later rung done with per-hit review. Not the same commit either way.

If you want the archive in too, I'd want it as a separate rung specifically so its diff can be read for transcription damage without 1680 mechanical edits in the way.

Four items now, and one is much bigger than the interludes:

- `0.77.3 docs: interlude shape` — define it, pull the four scattered facts under it
- `0.77.4 docs: jj describe drops ochid` — itself an interlude, demonstrating 0.77.3
- **`0.78.0 refactor: typeable punctuation in source and notes`** — ~1680 sites, mandatory cargo cycle, README regeneration. At that size with a real validation step it reads as a cycle with a ladder, not a patch interlude.

That pushes jj-lib to 0.79.0 and trapezoid-push to 0.80.0. Worth it, I think: calling a 1680-site change with a mandatory cargo cycle a patch bump would be the first interlude that isn't one, in the same breath as we're writing down what an interlude is.

Replace "Banned:" with something scoped to the act, e.g. "Never authored: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`", and scope the absoluteness clause: "Unlike the semicolon rule this one is absolute **for text we write**; transcribed text is not ours to change." That makes the specimen/use/transcription split a consequence of the rule rather than an exception carved out of it.

## The consequence that actually matters

chores-15 recorded two forward-looking items that both assume a checkable target:

- "The audit must enumerate the ban, not a memory of it"
- "A future `validate-repo` byte scan should read its character set from one place"

A byte scan **cannot** implement this rule. Presence is legitimate, so the target is not zero, and no scanner can tell an authored em dash from a transcribed one — that distinction lives in intent, not in bytes. Any checker written to the current wording will either report thousands of false positives or need an exception list that grows forever.

Two shapes that do work:

- **Baseline delta.** Record per-file counts; the check fails when a count *rises*. Authoring a new one trips it; transcriptions are inert once recorded. No classification needed, and it degrades gracefully — a legitimate new transcription is a one-line baseline update with a reviewer looking at it.
- **Structural exemption.** Require transcriptions to sit in fenced blocks, scan only outside them. Cleaner to check, but it's a new prose constraint and the specimens in AGENTS.md are inline spans, so it needs its own carve-out anyway.

I'd take the baseline delta. It matches what the rule actually is — a ratchet on new authoring — and it makes the sweep's value legible: converting the live surfaces lowers the baseline, and the archive's 1965 sites just sit in it, harmless, until touched.

That also settles your chores-archive question by making it moot: with a delta check, leaving the archive unconverted costs nothing, so "converts when touched" is the right policy and the sweep can stop at the live surfaces.

It adds a small amendment to whichever commit does the sweep, and it changes what Todo #3's neighborhood expects from `validate-repo`. Revised:

## Iterative work

When work for a single commit (the **target**) benefits
from incremental review, loop:

1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@` on top of the target.
2. Make the next round of changes.
3. User reviews the round (see
   [Reviewing changes](#reviewing-changes)).
4. `jj squash -R .` folds into the target and creates a
   new empty `@`.
5. If not done, go to step 2.

Same jj mechanics as a
[sub-cycle ladder](#sub-cycle-ladders), but at
single-commit scope, so the version doesn't change.

## Sub-cycle ladders

When a Work commit subdivides into a sub-cycle (see
[Numbering](#numbering) for suffix nesting), its Work
commits typically live as a local jj `@` chain and
**collapse into the sub-cycle's Close-out** before the
parent cycle continues. Ladder commits are scratch, for
review and bisection only.

### Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder

For each Work commit in the ladder:

1. `jj new -R .`: create a fresh empty `@`.
2. Do the commit's work.
3. Run the fast validation (Rust example: `cargo test
   --bins`). **Non-negotiable**, because for code, build and
   clippy alone miss regressions until a later commit runs the
   full suite, raising bisection cost.
4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: working title
   only; the sub-cycle Close-out collects everything
   into one final commit.

### Navigating the ladder

Common moves:

- `jj log -r '<base>::' -R .`: see the whole ladder
  from its base.
- `jj edit -r <prefix> -R .`: jump `@` to any ladder
  commit by chid prefix; useful for bisection.
- `jj edit @-- -R .`: quick-jump back two commits.
- `jj diff -r <chid> -R .`: review one commit in
  isolation.

Modifications to any ladder commit rewrite it in place;
descendants auto-rebase.

`<base>` is the parent of the first ladder commit; `-u`
keeps `@`'s description and discards the sources'.

intermediate commits are auto-abandoned.

Then `vc-x1 push <bookmark>` as for any other commit.

For N = 1 the squash is a no-op (`<base>..@-` is empty
when `@-` is `<base>`); push the single commit directly.

## docs: re-describe rule + defer punctuation sweep

Commits:

Two unrelated threads, both found by reading the `0.77.x`
ladder rather than by doing the work it planned: a `jj describe`
hazard that had been recorded only inside a feature request,
and two planned rungs whose value did not survive scrutiny.

- **Re-describing is coordinate-first.** `jj describe` on a
  published or already-stamped commit is a history rewrite and
  silently drops the `ochid:` trailer, since it replaces the
  whole message and nothing guards it the way `squash-push`
  guards a squash. The hazard is not theoretical: it cost the
  `0.77.2` amend its trailer, which survived only by
  hand-copying. AGENTS.md carries the rule, next to the ochid
  semantics rather than inside the Todo that will eventually
  fix it.
- **The sub-cycle ladder is the named exception**, and it
  needed saying from both ends. Ladder commits never leave the
  machine, so they carry no trailer and step 4's `describe` is
  first-time authoring, not a rewrite. cycle-protocol says so
  at the per-Work-commit contract and again at the Close-out
  squash, which is the ladder's single push and where the
  trailer is stamped.
- **`typically` became `will`** in the sub-cycle intro, since
  the local-only claim is flat and a hedge in the same section
  undercut it.
- **Two rungs left the ladder**: the `src` punctuation sweep to
  `## Todo`, interlude shape to the backlog.

### Wording strength should match the deviation it invites

The session hit the same calibration error twice, pointing
opposite ways, which is what made it visible.

- `Banned:` in the punctuation rule was too strong for a rule
  with legitimate exceptions, so the section spent four
  paragraphs contradicting its own first word.
- `typically` in the sub-cycle intro was too weak for a rule
  whose exception should be deliberate, letting a reader stray
  without noticing a choice had been made.

We think the useful test is not "is this rule absolute" but
"how much hesitation should breaking it cost". Any rule here
can be broken; the wording decides whether breaking it is an
act or a default.

### Why the source sweep left the ladder

The rule cannot be enforced at the byte level, and noticing
that changed the sweep's shape and its checker both.

- **`Banned` is not what the rule means.** Transcribed tool
  output and published commit titles keep their characters,
  so presence in a file is legitimate and the prohibition is
  on *authoring*. The rewording is now the first step of the
  `## Todo` entry, because it is what bounds the sweep.
- **Scope shrank to what carries forward.** `src/` and
  `tests/` (~875 sites, four characters, not the 655 em dashes
  the retired rung counted) convert; `notes/` (~805) and the
  chores archive (1965) stay under "converts when touched".
  The archive is thick with transcription that must not
  convert, and heading conversions move anchors the notes
  files link into.
- **A `validate-repo` byte scan cannot implement this**, since
  no scanner separates authored from transcribed. The backlog
  entry now asks for a per-file count baseline that fails on a
  rise, which supersedes the note two sections above asking
  the checker to read its character set from one place.

vc-x1 0.71.0

Commit both repos, push the work repo's BOOKMARK, and
squash-push the bot repo's `main` — one resumable command.

Collapses the manual commit-push-publish ceremony into a
single subcommand with two interactive approval gates and a
state machine with persistent progress so interruptions can
resume without re-doing completed stages.

Stages: preflight (tracking / bot-published / sync checks —
no build steps; run project checks yourself before pushing)
→ review (approve diff)
→ message ($EDITOR / --title+--body, approve text) →
commit-work → commit-bot (skipped if clean) → bookmark-set
(work repo → <bookmark>, bot repo → main) → push-work →
squash-push-bot. Failures in commit-work / commit-bot /
bookmark-set roll both repos back via
`jj op restore` to the snapshot recorded before commit-work.
After push-work succeeds the remote boundary is crossed and
recovery is forward-only.

Non-interactive use: pass both --title and --body plus --yes
to skip the review gate. Saved state carries title/body
across resumes so only the first invocation needs them.

Usage: vc-x1 push [OPTIONS] [BOOKMARK]

Arguments:
  [BOOKMARK]
          Bookmark to advance in the work repo (positional form of
          `--bookmark`). The bot repo always advances `main`.
          
          Accepting a positional lets the common case read as `vc-x1 push main`
          without the `--bookmark` ceremony; `--bookmark` is kept as an alias
          for scripts and for composition with other args. The two forms
          conflict if both supplied.

Options:
      --bookmark <BOOKMARK>
